title: Stakeholder Role-Effectiveness Mismatch in Mountain Land Governance: Evidence from a Tourism Pressured Himalayan Landscape
content: In mountain areas, tourism changes land use and puts development, environmental fragility and livelihoods at odds, and managing the competition is not always simple. The question this study poses is whether the stakeholders that communities consider to be central to land-use governance in the tourism-pressured Upper Beas Basin of Himachal Pradesh, India, are also found to be effective? The evidence is derived from a structured household survey conducted over three rounds of field visits, between 2024 and 2026, with 300 respondents across nine settlements. We created three composite measures from the Likert-scale responses: a Stakeholder Role Index (SRI), a Stakeholder Effectiveness Index (SEI) and a Community Perception Index (CPI); and calculated a Role-Effectiveness Mismatch (REM) as SRI – SEI. Friedman and Wilcoxon procedures were used to test for differences among the stakeholders, Kruskal-Wallis and Holm-adjusted Mann-Whitney tests were used to test for differences across the tourism contexts, and the results were compared with HC3 regression. The highest scores were achieved by local communities in both role (SRI = 3.435) and effectiveness (SEI = 3.268). The private sector had the highest positive mismatch (REM = +0.381), while the NGOs/Civil Society had the highest negative mismatch (REM = -0.420). The tourism context had little impact on SRI and SEI but was significant for CPI (H = 10.609, p = 0.005) with high and intermediate tourism settlements being significantly different. Overall, the analysis reveals that prominence in governance and perceived effectiveness are two separate dimensions and that REM offers a practical way to locate where-and for which actors-the two diverge in mountain land governance.
